sites.name: de Gerlache rim ridge
sites.summary: A well-lit ridge on the rim of de Gerlache crater, about 16 km from the named feature of NASA's de Gerlache Rim 2 candidate region.
processes: Cold trapping of volatiles in permanent shadow
limits: Earth's gravity is about 6 times the Moon's
The Moon has no atmosphere; Earth sites cannot reproduce vacuum
Permanently shadowed lunar craters reach far colder temperatures than anywhere on Earth

criteria.label: Sunlit time
criteria.rule: >= 50 % at the surface (ours; published 85-95 % is 2-10 m above ground)

criteria.label: Slope
criteria.rule: <= 10 deg (ours; Chandrayaan-3's lander was built for <= 12 deg)

criteria.label: Distance to permanent shadow
criteria.rule: <= 10 km to a shadowed area of >= 1 km2 (ours)

selection.note: Passes all four criteria; among the best-lit spots at the pole. It sits next to NASA's de Gerlache Rim 2 region (16.1 km from its named feature), which cross-checks our method against NASA's own choice.

sites.name: Shackleton-de Gerlache connecting ridge
sites.summary: The ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters, already known in the literature as one of the best-lit places at the south pole. Our screening found it independently.

sites.name: Cabeus-Malapert ridge
sites.summary: A ridge between the rim of Cabeus crater and Mons Malapert, outside NASA's candidate regions. Cabeus is where NASA's LCROSS impact found water ice in 2009; this spot is the best lit of our lunar candidates and keeps Earth in view most of the time.

sites.name: Chandrayaan-3
sites.summary: India's 2023 lander, one of the landings closest to the lunar south pole, on old highland terrain lit by a low Sun.
limits: Earth's gravity is about 6 times the Moon's
The Moon has no atmosphere; Earth sites cannot reproduce vacuum
Surface radiation on the Moon is far higher

criteria.label: Sunlit time
criteria.rule: >= 50 % at the surface (ours; published 85-95 % is 2-10 m above ground)
criteria.why: It was built to work for one lunar day, so it needed daylight for two weeks, not light all year. At 69° S the Sun rises and sets as it does on most of the Moon.

criteria.label: Slope
criteria.rule: <= 10 deg (ours; Chandrayaan-3's lander was built for <= 12 deg)

criteria.label: Distance to permanent shadow
criteria.rule: <= 10 km to a shadowed area of >= 1 km2 (ours) — none found within 30 km
criteria.why: It did not go to look for ice. No permanently shadowed area of 1 km² or more lies within 30 km.

selection.note: Fails sunlit time and distance to permanent shadow. That is not a fault of the site: the mission was built for a different job than the one our rules describe. The rule check gives the reason for each.

purpose.text: Chandrayaan-3 set out to show a safe, soft landing and a rover drive, and to run experiments on the surface, for one lunar day (about 14 Earth days). ISRO chose the site for gentle slopes, few boulders and craters, enough light for power and a clear line to Earth, in high southern latitudes that had hardly been explored.

sites.name: Southern Utopia Planitia
sites.summary: Smooth lowland plains in the south of Utopia Planitia, about 900 km east of where China's Zhurong rover landed. The point deepest inside the largest safe area on Mars.
limits: Earth's gravity is about 2.6 times Mars gravity
Mars air is about 100 times thinner and mostly CO2
Surface radiation on Mars is far higher

criteria.label: Air to slow down (est. surface pressure)
Albedo (second dust check)
criteria.rule: <= 0.25 where thermal inertia is below 150 (MSL, Mars 2020: bright and low-inertia = dusty)

selection.note: Passes every criterion inside a 4163 thousand km2 safe area, 108 km from its edge, and more than 500 km from any past landing. Second look at 463 m: 95 % of slopes below 0.31 deg, relief 37 m over 25 km (landings for comparison: InSight 0.53 deg / 90 m, Viking 1 0.94 deg / 72 m, Spirit 1.49 deg / 297 m).

sites.name: Curiosity (Gale crater)
sites.summary: NASA rover exploring the layered sediments of Mount Sharp inside Gale crater, a former lake basin.
limits: Earth's gravity is about 2.6 times Mars gravity
Mars air is about 100 times thinner and mostly CO2
Surface radiation on Mars is far higher

criteria.label: Air to slow down (est. surface pressure)
Albedo (second dust check)
criteria.rule: <= 0.25 where thermal inertia is below 150 (MSL, Mars 2020: bright and low-inertia = dusty)

criteria.label: Relief over ~18 km
criteria.why: The mountain it came to study stands inside our 18 km window. Curiosity's guided entry was built to land within 10 km of its target, so the flat crater floor beside the mountain was enough.

selection.note: Fails relief over ~18 km. That is not a fault of the site: the mission was built for a different job than the one our rules describe. The rule check gives the reason for each. Against the limits its own team set, it passes.

missionRules.label: Elevation (the mission's own limit)
missionRules.source: Golombek et al. 2012 (MSL); our MOLA elevation

purpose.text: Curiosity explores whether Mars could once have supported life. Gale crater was chosen for its potential as a former habitat: the rover climbs the layered mountain in its centre.

sites.name: Perseverance (Jezero crater)
sites.summary: NASA rover exploring an ancient river delta in Jezero crater, searching for signs of past life and caching samples.
limits: Earth's gravity is about 2.6 times Mars gravity

Albedo (second dust check)

criteria.label: Relief over ~18 km
criteria.why: The delta cliffs and the crater rim it came to study are inside our 18 km window (517 m against our limit of 500 m). The mission flew a new system that steers away from hazards during descent, so it could accept rougher ground.

selection.note: Fails relief over ~18 km. That is not a fault of the site: the mission was built for a different job than the one our rules describe. The rule check gives the reason for each. Against the limits its own team set, it passes.

missionRules.source: Fergason et al. 2017 (Mars 2020); our MOLA elevation

purpose.text: Perseverance seeks signs of ancient life and collects rock samples for a possible return to Earth. Jezero crater was chosen because it once held a lake fed by a river, whose delta is still there.
